name: AP English Literature and Composition
overview: AP English Literature and Composition trains students to read fiction, poetry, and drama closely and to write analytical arguments about literature. The course is built on six big ideas: character, setting, structure, narration, figurative language, and literary argumentation.
examMode: Fully digital in Bluebook (essays typed; responses auto-submit at the end)

sections.name: Section I
sections.notes: Questions are grouped in sets on 5 passages of prose fiction, poetry, and drama.

sections.name: Section II, Question 3
sections.notes: Students choose a work of literary merit to discuss.

skills.name: Character
skills.description: Explain how characters, their perspectives, and their changes contribute to meaning.

skills.name: Setting
skills.description: Explain the function of setting in a text.

skills.name: Structure
skills.description: Explain how plot, sequence, and form contribute to meaning.

skills.name: Narration
skills.description: Explain how narrators and speakers shape perspective.

skills.name: Figurative Language
skills.description: Explain how comparisons, imagery, and symbols convey meaning.

skills.name: Literary Argumentation
skills.description: Develop a defensible interpretation supported by textual evidence and commentary.

scoring.summary: Section I counts 45% and Section II 55%. Each essay is scored on a 6-point rubric: Row A thesis (1), Row B evidence and commentary (4), Row C sophistication (1). The weighted composite is converted to 1–5 using unpublished cut points.

frqTypes.name: Q3 Literary Argument
frqTypes.howScored: Thesis 1, evidence and commentary 4, sophistication 1; evidence comes from a work the student chooses.

strategy: Read each passage once for the whole before answering; many questions ask about shifts and overall effect.
Identify the speaker or narrator and their attitude before analyzing devices.
In essays, build a thesis that names the work's complexity (a tension, ambiguity, or shift), not just a list of devices.
Embed short quotations and explain how word choice creates meaning.
Prepare two or three rich novels or plays for Q3 that fit many prompts (identity, isolation, sacrifice, power).
Budget about 40 minutes per essay, with 5–8 minutes of planning.
pitfalls: Treating the speaker of a poem as the poet.
Choosing a Q3 work you know only from a film or summary.
Missing tonal shifts at volta or turning points.
Ignoring how form (stanza, line breaks, chronology) contributes to meaning.

caveats: Klutch wrote this profile from knowledge of the course framework without re-opening College Board pages in this session; recheck question counts, the number of answer choices, and timing against AP Central.
The CED numbers its nine units but they follow a spiral of short fiction, poetry, and longer works; titles here use that structure.
All practice passages are original works written for Klutch, not excerpts from published literature, so they can be freely used.
